title: Calibrated Explanations in Clinical AI Triage: Effects of Uncertainty Visualization on Radiologist Diagnostic Accuracy
short_title: Calibrated Explanations in Clinical AI Triage
authors: E. Vance, M. K. Patel, S. Lindqvist, H. Chen
venue: ACM CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI)
abstract: Clinical decision support systems increasingly rely on deep neural networks to prioritize thoracic radiographs in emergency triage workflows. However, uncalibrated saliency maps often induce over-reliance when model predictions are erroneous. In this paper, we investigate how calibrated uncertainty-aware explanations shape clinician-AI collaborative decision-making under time pressure. We conducted a randomized controlled study with N = 128 board-certified radiologists and emergency physicians across 1,920 diagnostic triage trials comparing three interfaces: unassisted reading, standard AI prediction with heatmap, and calibrated uncertainty intervals paired with counterfactual feature attributions. Results demonstrate that uncertainty-aware explanations improve clinician diagnostic accuracy by 14.2% (p < 0.001) over standard AI assistance and reduce false-positive over-reliance on out-of-distribution cases by 31.8%, while adding only 1.4 seconds to mean case review time. Despite strong internal validity, our evaluation is restricted to a single-institution retrospective chest radiograph dataset and does not measure longitudinal alert fatigue across multi-week shifts.
claim: Uncertainty-aware explanations improve clinician diagnostic accuracy by 14.2% and cut false-positive over-reliance by 31.8%.
limitation: Single-institution retrospective radiology dataset; does not evaluate longitudinal multi-week shift fatigue.

evidence_card.claim: Uncertainty-aware explanations improve clinician diagnostic accuracy by 14.2% and cut false-positive over-reliance by 31.8%.
evidence_card.limitation: Single-institution retrospective radiology dataset; does not evaluate longitudinal multi-week shift fatigue.

rationale: Rigorous empirical human-AI collaborative decision-making study with large human cohort (N = 128 >= 30) and quantitative task accuracy outcomes.

title: Kernel-Level KV-Cache Quantization for Sub-10ms Edge LLM Token Generation on Mobile NPUs
short_title: Kernel-Level KV-Cache Quantization for Edge LLMs
authors: J. Zhao, R. Subramanian, A. Kowalski
abstract: Deploying autoregressive large language models on memory-constrained mobile neural processing units (NPUs) is bottlenecked by key-value (KV) cache bandwidth during long-context prefill and decoding. We present FlashKV-4, a kernel-level asymmetric 4-bit group quantization scheme with fused dequantization-attention tiling specifically engineered for ARMv9 matrix extensions. Across four open-weight LLM families (Llama-3-8B, Mistral-7B, Qwen2-7B, and Gemma-7B) evaluated on LongBench and SpecBench hardware traces, FlashKV-4 reduces time-to-first-token (TTFT) latency by 2.8x and shrinks peak DRAM footprint by 68.4% with less than 0.3% perplexity degradation. While our systems benchmark demonstrates substantial throughput gains on embedded silicon, we do not conduct any human-in-the-loop interaction studies or evaluate end-user task performance.
claim: 4-bit group quantization reduces TTFT latency by 2.8x and memory footprint by 68.4% on mobile NPUs.
limitation: Pure hardware/systems latency benchmark; no human-in-the-loop evaluation or human participants (N = 0).

evidence_card.claim: 4-bit group quantization reduces TTFT latency by 2.8x and memory footprint by 68.4% on mobile NPUs.
evidence_card.limitation: Pure hardware/systems latency benchmark; no human-in-the-loop evaluation or human participants (N = 0).

rationale: Off-topic pure systems/hardware optimization benchmark with zero human participants (N = 0) and no human-AI decision task.

title: AI Co-Pilots for Financial Risk Auditing: An Exploratory Workplace Pilot on Collaborative Anomaly Triage
short_title: AI Co-Pilots for Financial Risk Auditing: A Pilot
venue: Workshop on Human-Centered FinTech & AI Decision Support
abstract: Financial compliance teams face growing pressure to audit thousands of cross-border ledger transactions for subtle money-laundering anomalies. Recent advances in conversational large language models promise to transform human-AI collaborative risk auditing by synthesizing transaction narratives on demand. In this paper, we introduce AuditMate, an interactive generative AI co-pilot integrated into an enterprise spreadsheet workflow for collaborative anomaly triage. To evaluate how AuditMate supports human decision makers in realistic compliance review, we observed a cohort of junior summer auditing interns (N = 4) over a two-hour informal think-aloud session without a baseline control condition. Participants uniformly reported feeling much faster and more confident when querying the AI co-pilot to summarize suspicious invoices, praising its conversational fluency. We did not track objective anomaly detection accuracy or false-negative rates, leaving controlled quantitative validation to future work.
claim: Analysts report feeling faster and more confident when using a conversational LLM audit assistant.
limitation: Extremely small unrepresentative sample (N = 4 < 10); subjective self-report only, no control group or quantitative accuracy metric.

evidence_card.claim: Analysts report feeling faster and more confident when using a conversational LLM audit assistant.
evidence_card.limitation: Extremely small unrepresentative sample (N = 4 < 10); subjective self-report only, no control group or quantitative accuracy metric.

rationale: Methodologically weak trap: topically framed around human-AI financial decision triage, but severely underpowered (N = 4 < 10), lacks a control group, and measures only subjective feelings rather than quantitative task performance.

title: Adaptive Reliance in Human-Swarm Search and Rescue: Balancing Operator Workload and Target Recovery
short_title: Adaptive Reliance in Human-Swarm Search & Rescue
authors: K. Nakamura, L. Okafor, B. G. Sterling
venue: ACM/IEEE International Conference on Human-Robot Interaction (HRI)
abstract: Human supervisors commanding autonomous drone swarms during disaster search-and-rescue operations frequently suffer from cognitive overload when validating noisy computer-vision target detections across multiple video feeds. We propose an adaptive autonomy allocation policy that dynamically shifts verification authority between the human operator and the swarm consensus model based on real-time operator pupillometry and environmental occlusion scores. In a within-subjects laboratory experiment with N = 64 trained emergency response operators across 384 simulated post-earthquake search missions, adaptive autonomy switching reduced NASA-TLX cognitive load scores by 24.5% and improved high-priority survivor recovery accuracy by 19.0% (p < 0.002) compared to fixed manual verification. A key limitation is that missions were conducted in a high-fidelity 2D/3D desktop simulation rather than physical outdoor field deployments.
claim: Adaptive autonomy switching reduces operator cognitive load by 24.5% and improves target recovery accuracy by 19.0%.
limitation: High-fidelity desktop simulation rather than physical outdoor drone field deployment.

evidence_card.claim: Adaptive autonomy switching reduces operator cognitive load by 24.5% and improves target recovery accuracy by 19.0%.
evidence_card.limitation: High-fidelity desktop simulation rather than physical outdoor drone field deployment.

rationale: Rigorous empirical within-subjects study (N = 64 >= 30) measuring quantitative human-AI collaborative target recovery performance and workload.

title: LLM-Simulated Personas as Proxies for Crowd Annotators in Content Moderation Triage
short_title: LLM-Simulated Personas as Proxies for Crowd Annotators
authors: S. Alvarez, Y. Park, N. Choudhury
venue: ACM Conference on Computer-Supported Cooperative Work and Social Computing (CSCW)
abstract: Moderating borderline hate speech requires reconciling diverse sociodemographic perspectives, a process traditionally studied through large human crowd panels. Here we explore whether ensembles of persona-conditioned large language models can approximate human annotator disagreement distributions and serve as decision-support signals for human moderators. We pair 500 synthetic LLM persona agents with a validation cohort of N = 18 human baseline raters evaluating 300 ambiguous social media posts. Synthetic persona ensembles correlate with human inter-rater variance at r = 0.71, and preliminary inspection suggests human raters occasionally revise borderline flags when shown persona disagreement histograms. However, because the human cohort is relatively small (N = 18) and the protocol mixes static ground-truth labeling with informal interactive inspection, full-text verification is needed to determine whether quantitative collaborative decision gains were isolated.
claim: Synthetic LLM persona ensembles approximate human disagreement on toxicity labels (r = 0.71) across 300 posts.
limitation: Small human cohort (N = 18, between 15 and 25); ambiguous whether protocol isolates interactive human-AI decision performance vs. static labeling.

evidence_card.claim: Synthetic LLM persona ensembles approximate human disagreement on toxicity labels (r = 0.71) across 300 posts.
evidence_card.limitation: Small human cohort (N = 18, between 15 and 25); ambiguous whether protocol isolates interactive human-AI decision performance vs. static labeling.

rationale: Borderline study (N = 18 falls in the N = 15-25 borderline range) with low extraction confidence (0.62) and methodological ambiguity between synthetic benchmark correlation and actual human-AI collaborative decision-making.

title: Prompt Ensembling for Zero-Shot Tabular Classification Across Heterogeneous Schemas
short_title: Prompt Ensembling for Zero-Shot Tabular Classification
authors: M. Lindholm, C. Wu, F. Benitez
abstract: Tabular classification in high-stakes domains such as credit scoring and hospital readmission prediction typically relies on gradient-boosted decision trees trained on task-specific labeled rows. We investigate whether zero-shot large language models can match supervised tree ensembles via automated serialization diversity and self-consistency voting. By generating twelve distinct markdown, JSON, and natural-language sentence templates per row and aggregating token log-probabilities, our zero-shot prompt ensemble outperforms tuned XGBoost baselines on 6 out of 15 UCI benchmark datasets without any gradient updates. All experiments are executed entirely offline across automated benchmark splits with N = 0 human participants, focusing purely on algorithmic classification AUC rather than interactive human decision support.
claim: Self-consistency voting over diverse tabular serializations beats tuned gradient boosting on 6/15 UCI datasets.
limitation: Purely automated offline ML inference; no human decision maker or user study involved (N = 0).

evidence_card.claim: Self-consistency voting over diverse tabular serializations beats tuned gradient boosting on 6/15 UCI datasets.
evidence_card.limitation: Purely automated offline ML inference; no human decision maker or user study involved (N = 0).

rationale: Off-topic pure machine learning benchmark on static UCI datasets with zero human participants (N = 0).

title: Over-Reliance on Confident AI Recommendations in Legal Discovery: A Controlled Study with Practicing Attorneys
short_title: Over-Reliance on Confident AI Recommendations in Legal Discovery
authors: R. Thorne, A. Goldstein, P. V. Iyer
venue: ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency (FAccT)
abstract: Generative legal discovery assistants increasingly display numerical confidence badges alongside privilege and responsiveness classifications during corporate litigation review. To test how uncalibrated confidence displays influence legal decision accuracy, we conducted a preregistered between-subjects experiment with N = 92 practicing JD attorneys and senior litigation paralegals reviewing 40 complex commercial contract clauses. When the AI model displayed uncalibrated high-confidence badges (>90%) on deceptive edge-case clauses where the underlying model was actually wrong, attorney automation bias errors increased by 27.4% (p < 0.001) compared to a badge-free evidence highlight interface. Introducing a mandatory pre-decision premise verification step restored accuracy to baseline while preserving a 34% speed advantage over manual review. Limitations include the use of self-contained contract vignettes rather than multi-day document repositories.
claim: Uncalibrated high-confidence AI badges increase lawyer automation bias errors by 27.4% on deceptive edge cases.
limitation: Vignette-based contract clauses rather than multi-day longitudinal discovery workflows.

evidence_card.claim: Uncalibrated high-confidence AI badges increase lawyer automation bias errors by 27.4% on deceptive edge cases.
evidence_card.limitation: Vignette-based contract clauses rather than multi-day longitudinal discovery workflows.

rationale: Directly relevant empirical between-subjects human-AI decision study with N = 92 domain experts (>= 30) and quantitative accuracy and speed outcomes.

title: Interactive Counterfactual Sliders for Loan Underwriting Decisions: Contesting Algorithmic Rejections
short_title: Interactive Counterfactuals for Loan Underwriting Decisions
authors: H. Lindqvist, G. Mensah, K. Verma
venue: ACM International Conference on Intelligent User Interfaces (IUI)
abstract: Credit underwriters working alongside automated risk-scoring models often struggle to determine when an algorithmic loan rejection reflects historical training bias versus genuine default risk. We designed CounterLoan, an interactive decision-support workspace featuring real-time counterfactual feature sliders that allow underwriters to test how plausible applicant adjustments alter model risk tiers. In an exploratory mixed-methods evaluation with N = 21 regional loan officers reviewing 16 synthetic and historical credit files, interactive counterfactual sliders helped participants accurately contest biased model rejections in 61.3% of disputed cases compared to 42.0% with static SHAP bar charts. However, because our sample size of N = 21 domain officers falls below the standard N >= 30 statistical power threshold and exhibits ceiling effects on non-disputed files, full-text inspection of the mixed-methods statistical reporting is required.
claim: Counterfactual sliders help loan officers accurately contest biased model rejections in 61.3% of disputed cases.
limitation: Sample size (N = 21) is below the N >= 30 inclusion threshold (falls in N = 15-25 borderline range); ceiling effect on easy cases.

evidence_card.claim: Counterfactual sliders help loan officers accurately contest biased model rejections in 61.3% of disputed cases.
evidence_card.limitation: Sample size (N = 21) is below the N >= 30 inclusion threshold (falls in N = 15-25 borderline range); ceiling effect on easy cases.

rationale: Borderline study: directly measures human-AI decision performance in loan underwriting, but sample size (N = 21) is in the 15-25 borderline tier requiring full-text review.
